Traducianism
truh-DOO-shuh-niz-um
n.
From Latin tradux, “a shoot or vine-branch trained for propagation,” hence ex traduce, “by propagation.” The view that the soul is propagated with the body from the parents.

📖 Biblical Definition

Traducianism is the view concerning the origin of the human soul which holds that the soul, like the body, is propagated from the parents in the act of generation—that each person receives both body and soul from his parents, the whole human being deriving by ordinary generation from Adam through the line of descent. It stands opposed to creationism (the soul-origin view), which holds that God immediately creates each individual soul and unites it to the body at conception or formation. Traducianists argue from several considerations. Scripture says God rested from His work of creation on the seventh day, suggesting He does not now create new souls daily, but works through the propagating powers He established. Man begets a son in his own likeness and image, the whole man reproducing after his kind, soul as well as body. Levi is said to have been ‘in the loins’ of Abraham, implying a real seminal presence of descendants in their forefathers. Above all, traducianism most readily explains the transmission of original sin and the corruption of nature: if the soul is propagated from fallen parents, then the whole man, soul and body, comes into the world bearing the corruption of Adam by natural descent, without God being charged with creating sinful souls. Creationists object that traducianism seems to make the soul divisible or material, and they prefer to safeguard the soul’s spiritual simplicity by immediate creation—though this raises the harder question of how a freshly created, pure soul comes to share Adam’s corruption. The debate is ancient and not settled by any church council; both views are held by the orthodox. Traducianism has been favored by many in the Reformed and Lutheran traditions precisely for its account of the unity of the race in Adam and the natural transmission of original sin, while creationism has appealed to those guarding the soul’s immateriality. The matter touches deep mysteries of the soul’s nature and origin, and is to be held with humility.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no entry for “traducianism,” but defines TRADUCE in its older sense of propagating or deriving by generation, the root of the doctrine.

expand to see more

TRADUCE, v.t. — ...In its older sense, to derive or propagate, as by generation; to transmit. Hence “traducianism,” the doctrine that the soul is propagated with the body from the parents.

The opposing view is creationism, that each soul is immediately created by God.

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 2:2 — "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made."

Genesis 5:3 — "And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth."

Hebrews 7:10 — "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him."

Psalm 51:5 — "Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This is an intramural debate between traducianism and creationism. Traducianism’s danger is the suggestion that the soul is divisible or material; creationism’s, the difficulty of how God creates a pure soul that shares Adam’s corruption.

expand to see more

The origin of the soul is a question the Scriptures do not decide with finality, and the church has never bound the conscience to either traducianism or creationism; both have been held by godly and orthodox theologians. The debate is therefore an intramural one, conducted over a genuine mystery, and to be carried on with humility rather than dogmatism. Traducianism commends itself chiefly by its account of the unity of the race in Adam and the natural transmission of original sin: if the whole man, soul and body, is propagated by generation, then every descendant comes into the world bearing Adam’s corruption through ordinary descent, and God is in no way charged with creating sinful souls.

Each view bears a difficulty the other presses. Against traducianism, creationists object that the propagation of the soul seems to imply that the soul is divisible or material—that a portion is passed from parent to child—which appears to compromise the soul’s spiritual simplicity and immateriality. Against creationism, traducianists press the harder question: if God immediately creates each soul pure and new, how does that freshly created soul come to share the corruption of Adam? Either God creates it already corrupt (which seems to make Him the author of sin), or He creates it pure and it is corrupted by union with a fallen body (which seems to locate sin in the body rather than the soul, or to make God the agent who joins a pure soul to certain corruption). The traducian account avoids this by deriving the whole fallen man from his parents. Neither view is free of mystery, and the wise course is to hold the certain truths—that every man is soul and body, that all descend from Adam, and that all inherit his corruption—while confessing that the precise manner of the soul’s origin lies among the secret things that belong to God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The view holds the soul comes ex traduce (by propagation, from the vine-shoot), the whole man begotten in the parent’s likeness and image, against immediate creation.
